name: Papaya enzyme hair inhibitor

card.summary: Folk idea that papaya's papain enzyme slows hair regrowth; the enzyme is real, the hair claim has no published trials behind it.
card.aka: Papain hair inhibitor, papaya hair-growth retardant
card.note: The FDA acted against unapproved topical papain drug products in 2008 after allergic reaction reports; latex allergy may raise risk.

quick.overview:
Papain is a protein-digesting enzyme from papaya, used in meat tenderisers, wound debridement and some cosmetics. A folk and cosmetic-marketing idea holds that applying papaya or papain can weaken hair or slow regrowth after removal.

No published study located tested this claim.
quick.mechanism: Papain is a cysteine protease that breaks down proteins. Proponents reason that it could degrade hair protein or follicle structures; this has not been tested in published human studies.
quick.risks: In 2008 the US FDA moved against marketing of unapproved topical papain drug products, citing reports of allergic reactions causing low blood pressure and rapid heart rate. People with latex allergy may be at higher risk of reacting to topical papain.

lead: The papaya enzyme hair inhibitor is the idea that applying papaya, or its enzyme papain, to the skin after hair removal slows regrowth, so smooth skin lasts longer between waxing or epilation sessions. It appears in post-wax products marketed as hair-regrowth retardants, and the claim also circulates as a home remedy.[2]

Papain, also called papaya proteinase I, is a cysteine protease from papaya (Carica papaya). It has established uses in meat tenderizers, wound debridement, cosmetics and other industries.[1] Product marketing describes papain as having long been used to prolong hair removal results; one retailer's blog post on a post-epilation papaya concentrate cites no study for this.[2] Proponents' reasoning is that a protein-digesting enzyme might weaken hair or follicle structures.
No published human trial of papain or papaya for slowing hair regrowth was found, and Wikipedia's papain article does not discuss hair products.[1]

chain: Papaya or papain product is applied after waxing
Enzyme is claimed to act on hair or follicle
Hair is claimed to return more slowly, extending smooth skin
angle.text: Users apply papaya-based products after hair removal hoping to extend the smooth period between sessions. The effect is claimed by product marketing rather than demonstrated in trials.

infobox: FDA action on unapproved topical papain drugs, 2008 [1]

paras: Papain is the namesake of the papain-like protease family. Beyond food and cosmetics, it is used to dissociate tissue in cell-culture work and in Papacarie, a gel for removing tooth decay without drilling.[1] Wikipedia lists cosmetics as one of several industries using the enzyme, without describing hair-related uses.[1]

A retailer's post on a papaya-and-vitamin-E post-epilation ampoule says the product helps slow hair regrowth and describes papain as long used to prolong the effects of hair removal; the post gives no study or results.[2]

On September 23, 2008, the US FDA warned companies to stop marketing topical papain drug products sold without approval, citing reports of serious drops in blood pressure with increased heart rate. People allergic to latex can also be allergic to papaya, so those with latex sensitivity may face a higher risk of reaction to topical papain.[1]
No studies found testing papain or papaya for slowing hair regrowth.

timeline.event: US FDA warns firms to stop marketing unapproved topical papain drug products.[1]
